segments.en: It's early on a Sunday morning, and smoke is curling up from behind the houses. Families are heating stones for the umu, an oven built on the ground, where taro and breadfruit will cook slowly while everyone goes to church.

Talofa, and hello from Samoa, a group of green volcanic islands in the middle of the South Pacific. The two biggest are Upolu, where the capital Apia sits by the harbour, and Savai'i, larger, quieter and wilder.
Life here follows fa'a Samoa, the Samoan way. It's built around the aiga, the extended family, respect for elders, sharing, and the matai, the chiefs chosen by each family to lead and speak for them.

Look at the traditional houses, called fale. Many are round or oval, with a thatched roof on wooden posts and no walls at all, so the sea breeze can flow through. When it rains, woven blinds are simply rolled down.

If you're invited in, sit cross-legged on the mat and try not to point your feet at anyone. And in the early evening, villages fall quiet for sa, a time of family prayer, called by a bell or a blown conch shell.
Back to that Sunday umu. After church comes to'ona'i, the big family lunch. You might taste palusami, young taro leaves baked in thick coconut cream, soft and rich and delicious.

Samoans have an ancient art of tattooing called tatau, and the English word tattoo is thought to come from Polynesian languages like this. A man's traditional tattoo, the pe'a, covers him from waist to knee and is a mark of great respect.
Dance is joyful here. In the siva, a graceful dancer tells a story with her hands, while in the fire knife dance, performers spin a blazing blade with amazing skill.
The islands are full of natural wonders. At To Sua, a long wooden ladder takes you down into a deep turquoise swimming hole, and on Savai'i, blowholes shoot sea water high into the air.
The Scottish writer Robert Louis Stevenson, who wrote Treasure Island, spent his last years here. Samoans called him Tusitala, the teller of tales, and his house at Vailima is now a museum.
And sport? Rugby is a passion, and the national team, Manu Samoa, performs its own fierce challenge dance, the siva tau, before every match.
Fa'afetai, thank you, for spending the morning with us. Sail south across the ocean, and the kingdom of Tonga, our old Polynesian neighbour, is waiting to greet you.
